We present INTERVenE, a family of Transformer architectures whose input is an interval-based, knowledge-based temporal abstraction (KBTA), a token stream of named clinical concepts (states, trends, events, contexts) drawn from a curated medical ontology, rather than an unnamed bin index or a raw measurement triplet. This naming layer is what we ask KBTA to do: it makes the model's per-token attributions resolve to clinical concepts by construction. INTERVenE offers two complementary variants: an auto-regressive decoder that generates future abstraction trajectories with a per-step risk readout (localizing \emph{when} and \emph{after which events} risk rises), and a bidirectional encoder for single-pass joint risk and time-to-event prediction. On 57,078 MIMIC-IV admissions, INTERVenE-Enc outperformed GRU-D, STraTS, and KarmaLego, reaching a support-weighted AUPRC of 0.672 ($+0.046$ over the strongest neural baseline, with non-overlapping 95\% bootstrap CIs), AUROC of 0.901, and length-of-stay MAE of 44.4\,h. INTERVenE-Ar complements these predictions with generated abstraction trajectories and evolving risk scores, achieving AUROC of 0.854 and AUPRC of 0.588 under the harder generative readout. An alternative-discretization ablation preserved predictive performance, supporting KBTA's role as a clinically named attribution substrate rather than a prerequisite for accuracy.
  </details>

- **[Calibration-Preserving Pruning: Compression as a Reliability Contract](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.23744)**  `arXiv:2608.23744`  
  _Ibne Farabi Shihab, Adria Binte Habib, Joyanta Jyoti Mondal_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Split conformal prediction, not the pruning rule, supplies finite-sample marginal coverage once a pruned model is fixed independently of the conformal calibration split. We study the separate efficiency problem: can pruning preserve score geometry well enough to obtain smaller valid prediction sets? Calibration-Preserving Pruning (CPP) augments a base pruning score with nonconformity-gradient saliency and uses disjoint pruning, validation-selection, conformal-calibration, and test splits. Bounded score perturbations imply bounded conformal-quantile shifts and controlled set inflation, but do not make the generic coverage theorem CPP-specific. Final five-seed Qwen2.5-1.5B results at 50\% sparsity show the largest gains on large-label tasks. On DBpedia-14, CPP-SparseGPT reduces mean set size from \(10.1\) to \(8.6\) while changing accuracy from \(0.347\) to \(0.366\); CPP-Wanda reduces \(11.2\) to \(9.0\) with an accuracy trade-off from \(0.310\) to \(0.295\). Across 15 dataset--sparsity cells, CPP-SparseGPT produces smaller sets in 13 and higher accuracy in 11. Matched controls show that generic supervised gradients explain much of the gain: true-label CPP is not statistically resolved from matched Wanda+SNIP, whereas threshold-aware candidate-label CPP reaches \(7.8\) mean set size at explicit accuracy and offline-compute costs. RoBERTa-base and Llama-3-8B diagnostics support transfer, but our claims remain limited to reliability-sensitive classification.
  </details>

- **[PureTD: Reinforcement Learning for Backgammon Money Games with No Evaluation-time Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15146)**  `arXiv:2608.15146`  
  _Alexander L. Strehl_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We revisit Tesauro's TD-Gammon for backgammon money games in the setting of no evaluation-time search. Both checker play and cube action (use of the doubling cube) are learned from scratch via self-play reinforcement learning (RL), with minimal hand-coded logic and no expert features. In this setting, we demonstrate that pure self-play RL suffices to train models that reach near-state-of-the-art playing strength. Specifically, for cubeful money games, our search-free model evaluates faster and is substantially stronger than the open-source engines GNU Backgammon and Open Sage running a one-move (1-ply) look-ahead search. Our method of training a cubeful model also outperforms the standard approach of training a cubeless model and deriving cubeful equity with Janowski-style formulas, when the two models are equally sized.
  </details>

- **[Towards Reliable Context Compression for Long-Horizon Agents: An Empirical Study of Execution Instability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06503)**  `arXiv:2608.06503`  
  _Guanghui Min, Liang Wu, Mayank Darbari, Chen Chen, Liangjie Hong_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Recurrent context compression controls context growth in long-horizon agents, but its behavioral effects remain poorly understood. In this preliminary empirical study, we show that compression can weaken the influence of recent interactions, increasing blocked actions, repeated exploration, and instability across runs. Motivated by these observations, we introduce TRACE, a verifier-guided framework that evaluates individual compaction events through paired closed-loop continuations from the same environment state and uses summary preferences to optimize a natural-language compression prompt while keeping all models frozen. Initial results on AppWorld show improvements over existing compression baselines in task performance, multi-run reliability, and context--execution efficiency. These findings provide early evidence for boundary-local evaluation as a promising direction for reliable agent context compression.
  </details>

- **[Multi-Modal, Multi-Temporal Geospatial Foundation Models Improve Global Above-Ground Biomass Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04792)**  `arXiv:2608.04792`  
  _Ghjulia Sialelli, Linus Scheibenreif, Jan Dirk Wegner, Konrad Schindler_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Accurate estimation of above-ground biomass (AGB) from satellite imagery is essential for the large-scale monitoring of carbon stocks, yet it remains a challenging regression task at global scale. Geospatial Foundation Models (GFMs) have recently emerged as a promising machine learning paradigm to derive general-purpose representations from Earth observation (EO) data, but their utility for quantitative regression tasks like biomass estimation remains largely unexplored, as most benchmarks focus on classification and segmentation. Here, we benchmark 13 GFMs for above-ground biomass estimation, specifically GEDI L4A biomass values. We compare them against a fully supervised state-of-the-art (SOTA) baseline trained on A Global-scale Biomass Dataset (AGBD), a machine learning-ready benchmark spanning diverse biomes and geographies. Most of the GFMs evaluated substantially underperform with respect to the supervised baseline, whether frozen or fine-tuned; only TESSERA and AlphaEarth Foundations (AEF) features with certain prediction heads yield a better performance. Our SOTA model trained on AEF embeddings and selected raw EO features achieves the best overall result (RMSE of 50.79 Mg/ha vs. 53.73 Mg/ha on AGBD features). This feature combination also generalizes better than AGBD features: it reduces RMSE by up to 25% in selected regions excluded from training, and, trained on single-year data alone, it outperforms the model trained on multi-year AGBD features. With labels from only 11 regions around the world, the AEF-based model also performs on par with the globally calibrated ESA CCI biomass product on independent reference plots. These findings indicate that GFM features can be highly informative for biomass estimation, when the underlying model is trained on rich multi-modal data.
  </details>

- **[Flow Matching with Missing Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28698)**  `arXiv:2607.28698`  
  _Fairoz Nower Khan, Nabuat Zaman Nahim, Peizhong Ju_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Flow matching assumes fully observed training data, which many real-world applications rarely provide. We study Missing-Data Flow Matching, which treats the missing coordinates of training samples as latent variables and averages the flow matching loss over the values they could take. We first prove that the oracle correction is exact: completing from the true pattern-conditioned posterior recovers the complete-data flow-matching objective under any missingness mechanism. Under missing completely at random (MCAR) and missing at random (MAR), this posterior equals the ordinary complete-data conditional, while under missing not at random (MNAR) it generally depends on the missingness mechanism and may require additional structure to identify. Our finite-sample analysis then answers design questions that the algorithm leaves open. Missingness transfers estimator variance rather than adding it, and for the fixed-parameter loss estimator one completion per example matches complete-data variance and is optimal under a fixed evaluation budget. A learned completion model contributes population completion bias, which we bound by its expected conditional Wasserstein distance to the true completion law. Experiments numerically validate the theoretical predictions, show that deterministic rather than frozen imputation reduces generated conditional variability, and place our method alongside strong classical and deep imputation baselines on real tabular data.
  </details>

- **[Circuit Claims Depend on What Is Extracted and How It Is Compared](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.18921)**  `arXiv:2607.18921`  
  _Yang Sheng, Jie Fu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Circuit extraction identifies model components whose presence preserves a target behavior under ablation, but preserving behavior does not single out one circuit. We study this in a synthetic Lean tactic-prediction benchmark with fixed proof rules and randomized surface form. Across dense and weight-sparse checkpoints of the same transformer, evaluated on atomic and compositional proofs, we vary which extracted object is reported: a compact prediction-preserving circuit, a broader graph retaining surrounding read, write, and routing structure, or a subgraph extracted with a post-ablation loss budget. First, overlap between groups of component-to-component connections is low, sometimes close to a random baseline. Overlap is much higher for selected attention-head sets under deterministic selection, but falls sharply when selection among equally scored heads is randomized. Second, the normalized graph-size ranking of conditions that differ in which supervised checkpoint initializes reinforcement learning (RL) agrees between repeated extractions of the compact circuit and between joint and separate query/key representations of each of the other two graphs. For the loss-budgeted graph, query/key ordering agreement persists through the budget sweep. Finally, across those same conditions, the largest exact-match accuracy gains from RL on compositional proofs come with the largest proportion of components in the compositional circuit that lie outside the corresponding atomic circuits. Ablating these additional components in the sparse RL model reduces compositional accuracy while largely preserving accuracy on the corresponding atomic tasks. A circuit-level claim therefore requires specifying which circuit is reported and how it is extracted and compared; behavior alone does not determine its interpretation. We distill these requirements into a reporting practice for circuit-extraction studies.
  </details>

- **[HarnessMDP: Learning to Control LLM Agent Harnesses with Offline Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.05458)**  `arXiv:2607.05458`  
  _Haiwen Yi, Xinyuan Song_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  The execution harness is a critical component of LLM agents, shaping how the agent interacts with its environment and organizes multi-step execution. Prior work has shown that improving tools, workflows, and other harness components can substantially improve agent performance. This suggests that the harness can be treated as a learnable control layer that adapts execution decisions from experience, rather than as a predetermined execution configuration. In this work, we introduce HarnessMDP, a learning-based framework that makes harness control itself learnable. HarnessMDP formulates agent execution as a finite-horizon Markov decision process, where the harness learns to select structural execution actions from the evolving agent state. The harness policy is learned offline from collected trajectories using task performance and deployed online to adaptively control new executions. Extensive experiments on coding tasks, $\tau$-bench, AgentBench, and other agent evaluation settings show that HarnessMDP consistently improves execution behavior and final task performance over baseline harnesses. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of HarnessMDP and establish learnable harness control as a practical mechanism for improving LLM agents through better execution. Our code is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[UniWind: Day-Ahead Wind Power Forecasting via Physics-Informed State Routing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01670)**  `arXiv:2607.01670`  
  _Ronghui Xu, Tongxin Wu, Guozhen Zhang, Yihan Li, Chenjuan Guo, Bin Yang, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Accurate day-ahead wind power forecasting is essential for cost-effective power-system operation. Wind power generation is primarily driven by future meteorological conditions while retaining temporal dependencies in power generation. In practice, observed wind-farm power reflects both meteorology-driven generation potential and deviations associated with local environmental and operational factors. Existing physical models provide useful constraints but adapt poorly across wind farms, whereas data-driven models can capture rich correlations but do not explicitly structure these two sources of variation. To bridge this gap, we propose UniWind, a wind power forecasting framework that integrates physics-informed generation priors with data-driven state-aware corrections. UniWind first employs a Physical Prior Estimator to construct a site-calibrated physical prior by combining a site-conditioned monotone warp with a shared physical power curve. It further applies a physical upper-bound constraint to shape this prior as a soft envelope of available wind power generation. UniWind then uses a Latent State Encoder to construct latent power-state representations from historical prior-power discrepancies and future meteorological context, and transforms the physical prior into final power forecasts through a State-aware Power Corrector with pseudo-label-guided routing and bounded expert correction. Experiments on 24 real-world datasets demonstrate UniWind's strong forecasting accuracy, robustness, and generalization across full-shot, cross-farm zero-shot, and cross-region zero-shot settings.
  </details>

- **[Stabilizing Extrapolation in Looped Transformers via Learned Stochastic Stopping](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.29983)**  `arXiv:2606.29983`  
  _Hsun-Yu Kuo, El Mahdi Chayti, Patrik Reizinger, Wieland Brendel, Martin Jaggi_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Looped Transformers, which repeatedly apply a shared transformer block, are an architecturally natural fit for variable-length algorithmic tasks. Although they can exhibit strong length generalization beyond the length of training sequences, this behavior is brittle, yielding high out-of-distribution (OOD) variance, even across well-performing in-distribution solutions. We trace this variance to the spurious correlation in simple algorithmic tasks between sequence length and number of loops. Introducing stochasticity into the number of loops during training sharply reduces OOD variance and stabilizes predictions across inference-time loop counts. To improve upon heuristic randomization schemes, we further analyze RL-Halting as a learned stochastic schedule and find that it generally improves the accuracy-stability trade-off. Across binary addition, Dyck-1, Unique Set, and Copy, learned stochastic stopping often improves this trade-off but can also stabilize a suboptimal computation. Our work suggests that "when to stop" should be treated as a training-time design choice, not merely an inference-time computation-allocation rule.
  </details>

- **[Symbolic Mechanistic Data Attribution: Tracing Training Influence to Learned Behavioral Policies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.29171)**  `arXiv:2606.29171`  
  _Reza Habibi, Darian Lee, Magy Seif El-Nasr_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  While existing data attribution methods can identify which training examples build specific mechanistic circuits, they cannot explain how training data shapes the behavioral decisions a model learns. We introduce Symbolic Mechanistic Data Attribution (SMDA), a framework that attributes training pairs to the interpretable symbolic policies governing model behavior. SMDA fits a closed-form Ridge regression over sparse autoencoder (SAE) features to model a behavior, then decomposes how each supervised fine-tuning (SFT) example shifts that policy through feature-activation ($\Delta X$) and output-probability ($\Delta Y$) pathways. We distill a symbolic policy for refusal in Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and analyze 200 SFT pairs. Our analysis reveals (1)~the symbolic policy's coefficients expose systematic gaps in the base model's safety behavior, such as religious stereotyping; (2)~per-feature $\Delta X/\Delta Y$ decomposition mechanistically explains why harmful and harmless pairs exert qualitatively different influences on certain features; and (3)~individual pairs routinely exhibit cross-feature interference, allowing SMDA to identify pairs whose dominant effect falls on unintended features. Retraining without such pairs improved accuracy by up to 4.5 percentage points over full fine-tuning. These results show that combining mechanistic interpretability with data attribution yields a diagnostic tool both more fine-grained than black-box influence functions and more scalable than manual circuit analysis.
  </details>

- **[Let's Ask Gauss: Improved One-Run Privacy Auditing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.12733)**  `arXiv:2606.12733`  
  _Adya Agrawal, Yu Wei, Jaspal Singh, Malik Magdon-Ismail, Vassilis Zikas_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Privacy auditing provides an important safeguard by estimating the actual information leaked by a model, thus ensuring that theoretical privacy guarantees hold in practice. We study empirical privacy auditing for differentially private (DP) machine learning, focusing on efficient one-run methods for mechanisms such as DP-SGD. Prior one-run approaches threshold training examples or "canaries" into binary membership guesses, which discards useful information. We show that, in the white-box DP-SGD setting, canary-aligned signals naturally form a sequence of random variables whose normalized sum is asymptotically Gaussian. We show that this gaussian perspective can also be naturally extended to other composition mechanisms that satisfy a classical, triangular-array, or martingale central limit theorem. Leveraging this distributional perspective, we develop a DP-auditing framework that leads to tighter privacy lower bounds from a single training run.
  </details>

- **[When to Align, When to Predict: A Phase Diagram for Multimodal Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.11190)**  `arXiv:2606.11190`  
  _Ilay Kamai, Hugues Van Assel, Aviv Regev, Hagai B. Perets, Randall Balestriero_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Cross-modal alignment (CA) and cross-modal prediction (CP) are the dominant paradigms for multimodal representation learning, yet there is no systematic understanding of when each succeeds and when each fails, a gap that leaves practitioners, especially in scientific domains with heterogeneous instruments and multiple levels of measurement, unable to diagnose why standard methods underperform the best single modality. We study both objectives under a spiked signal-plus-noise model with structured cross-modal nuisance correlation, the ingredient that breaks the classical recovery guarantees, and derive separation ratios that expose complementary failure modes: alignment whitens each modality and fails when nuisance is strongly correlated across views; prediction encodes whatever is cross-predictable through a one-sided whitening, with recovery governed by source-modality quality. The resulting phase diagram partitions multimodal problems into four regimes --- Both, CA only, CP only, and Neither --- refined by a recovery count that separates partial recovery from complete failure. We present a data-driven procedure to locate real-world datasets in this diagram using a small labeled subsample, identifying the preferred objective and prediction direction before any cross-modal training, and identifying when no objective in the CA/CP family can improve on the stronger modality alone. Experiments on synthetic data, stereo-vision benchmarks, image--caption pairs, and two real scientific domains, astronomy and single-cell multi-omics, validate the predictions in the nonlinear regime, including both faces of the Neither regime. Code to reproduce the results is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Structure-Preserving Correction Learning for Sparse Bayesian Inference in Brain Source Imaging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.07196)**  `arXiv:2606.07196`  
  _Marco Morik, Xiao Ruiting, Shinichi Nakajima, Stefan Haufe, Ismail Huseynov_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Classical sparse Type-II Bayesian methods for M/EEG brain imaging support joint estimation of source and noise hyperparameters, but rely on fixed iterative update rules. Although these updates are principled and interpretable, their dynamics are not data-driven. We propose to learn the update mechanism itself while preserving the underlying Bayesian structure by unfolding a classical joint hyperparameter-learning solver into a trainable neural network architecture whose layers mirror the original iterations. The resulting framework is initialized to recover the classical solver exactly before training and is enriched through progressively more expressive residual correction learning mechanisms, ranging from learnable biases to adaptive multilayer perceptron and attention-based contextual refinements. In this way, training does not replace Bayesian inference with a black-box predictor, but instead learns structured correction terms while retaining the interpretability and model-based character of the original update dynamics. Structured correction learning therefore aims to improve empirical reconstruction performance without replacing the original model-based inference mechanism. Experimental results show that the learned correction variants improve reconstruction performance and convergence behavior over the baseline unfolded solver while preserving its algorithmic transparency.
  </details>

- **[Rethinking Calibration for High-Sparsity LLM Pruning: From Single Sources to Capability Coverage](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.03328)**  `arXiv:2606.03328`  
  _Hu Xu, Zhaolong Xing, Congcong Liu, Jiaxing Wang, Zhida Jiang, Junshi Huang, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Post-training LLM pruning relies on a small calibration set, usually chosen heuristically and judged by WikiText perplexity or by mean accuracy on general-domain commonsense benchmarks. This single-axis view hides capability-specific effects: at 60\% sparsity, strategies separated by $2.85$ points in averaged commonsense accuracy diverge by $51.9$ points in code retention, and across 15 sources no single one preserves all capabilities. We treat calibration as a capability-coverage problem. Balanced, a uniform four-way mixture under a fixed budget, tests the principle on real corpora: it outperforms every evaluated single source, and its margin over C4 grows from $+4.6$ points at 30\% sparsity to $+18.8$ at 60\%. The advantage holds across model scale and a second model family, and transfers to held-out benchmarks disjoint from calibration construction. When aligned corpora are unavailable, IGSP approximates that mixture from the base model and the evaluation taxonomy alone, outperforming prior self-generation methods by $7.23$--$12.79$ points on the LLaMA main suite. On Qwen2.5-7B, IGSP exceeds Balanced on both the main suite and held-out benchmarks. Capability coverage is a first-order design variable for high-sparsity pruning.
  </details>

- **[Linear Strategic Classification with Endogenous Improvements](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.01198)**  `arXiv:2606.01198`  
  _Siddharth Shrivastava, Mahvith Akshintala, B Vamsha Vardhan Reddy, Naresh Manwani, Sujit Gujar, Ganesh Ghalme_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Classical models of strategic classification treat agents' responses to a deployed classifier as cosmetic: features change, but true labels do not. We study an improvement-aware variant in which strategic responses can change outcomes: agents choose post-deployment features strategically at a cost, and labels are then drawn from a fixed conditional outcome law. We formalize this problem for linear classifiers under a single-index qualification model and linear-decomposable costs. Under these assumptions, agents' best responses reduce to a closed-form shift of the decision boundary, and the resulting improvement-aware classification problem is learnable with linear sample complexity. As post-deployment labels are unavailable a priori, we begin by establishing a generalization bound with oracle access to the outcome law. One of our main contributions is a practical plug-in algorithm that replaces the oracle with an estimate, together with a bound on its improvement-aware error. We also show that the optimal classifier for standard strategic classification is a better proxy for the improvement-aware objective than the non-strategic Bayes-optimal classifier. Experiments on semi-synthetic and synthetic data support these findings and the plausibility of our assumptions.
  </details>

- **[Amortized Factor Inference Networks for Posterior Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.26419)**  `arXiv:2605.26419`  
  _Joohwan Ko, Justin Domke_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Amortized inference promises fast test-time Bayesian inference, but existing methods typically target a fixed model or a restricted model family. Extending amortization to new model families often requires retraining or test-time fine-tuning. In this paper, we ask: is it possible to build a single inference network capable of generalizing across varying priors, likelihoods, latent dimensions, and observation counts? We introduce Amortized Factor Inference Networks (AFINs), which describe a model as a list of typed prior and likelihood factors and map this description, together with the observations, to a Gaussian posterior approximation through an encode--merge--decode network whose learned parameters do not depend on the latent dimension or the number of observations. Experiments on synthetic and real-data benchmarks show that a single trained AFIN provides competitive posterior approximations at substantially lower test-time cost than NUTS and per-task variational inference. Optional importance sampling can further improve accuracy.
  </details>

- **[ChaosBench-Logic v2: Evaluating LLM Logical Reasoning over Dynamical Systems at Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.24305)**  `arXiv:2605.24305`  
  _Noel Thomas_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Standard accuracy on binary reasoning benchmarks hides critical failure modes: prior collapse, inconsistency under paraphrase, and inability to reason about parameter-dependent dynamics. We present ChaosBench-Logic v2, a 40,886-question benchmark over 165 dynamical systems with 27 FOL predicates and 78 axiom edges, together with CARE (Calibration- and Adversarial-Robust Evaluation), a protocol that surfaces these pathologies. Evaluating 14 models, we find that regime-transition reasoning remains near random (MCC = 0.05) even for frontier models, whereas FOL deduction with given premises reaches MCC = 0.52. Per-family decomposition shows that the proprietary-model advantage concentrates on cross-indicator (+0.40) and consistency tasks, while open-source Qwen 2.5-32B dominates indicator diagnostics (0.91 vs. 0.45). Two models exhibit negative MCC on bifurcation questions, confirmed as systematic anti-correlation via confusion-matrix analysis.
  </details>

- **[Evolutionary Multi-Task Optimization for LLM-Guided Program Discovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.22613)**  `arXiv:2605.22613`  
  _Halil Alperen Gozeten, Xuechen Zhang, Emrullah Ildiz, Ege Onur Taga, Tara Javidi, Samet Oymak_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Recent LLM-guided evolutionary search methods have shown that iterative program mutation can discover strong algorithms, but they typically optimize each task independently, even when related tasks share reusable structure. We study evolutionary multitask optimization (EMO) for LLM-guided program discovery and propose EMO-STA (Shared-Then-Adapt), a two-stage framework that first evolves a shared archive of executable programs across a task family and then adapts selected shared candidates to each target task. Within EMO-STA, we explore multiple adaptation strategies, including warm-starting from the shared archive, adapting the best average shared program, and adapting the shared program that performs best on each target task. Across eight task families spanning continuous optimization, geometric construction, modeling, and algorithmic optimization, EMO-STA improves over single-task evolution under matched evolutionary-iteration budgets in most settings, with STA Best-Local providing the strongest in-distribution adaptation and STA Best-Shared yielding robust transfer to unseen tasks. Iteration-allocation experiments show that devoting a substantial fraction of the family-level iteration budget to shared evolution is effective, with roughly balanced shared and aggregate adaptation budgets often yielding the best performance. ARC and time-series feature-engineering case studies further suggest that shared evolution can mitigate overfitting in low-evidence settings by favoring programs that perform well across related tasks rather than exploiting brittle task-specific artifacts.
  </details>

- **[Neurodata Without Boredom: Benchmarking Agentic AI for Data Reuse](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.12808)**  `arXiv:2605.12808`  
  _Ling-Qi Zhang, Kristin Branson_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Neuroscience data are fragmented across labs, experimental paradigms, and storage formats, and data reuse often requires substantial manual effort. Standardized formats have been proposed in response, but a fundamental tension persists: formats flexible enough for diverse experiments are rarely self-explanatory, while fully descriptive datasets demand documentation and curation effort that few labs can sustain. Coding agents, which can read code and text quickly with apparent attention to details humans tend to skim, are a natural candidate to reduce this burden. To measure how well coding agents perform data reuse, we benchmark them on eight recent papers with large-scale mouse neural recordings spanning diverse recording modalities, behavioral paradigms, and formats. Given the data, code, and paper, the agents must reformat the data for a common downstream task: training a decoder from neural activity to task and behavioral variables. Evaluating the resulting solutions, however, is challenging, since many conversion decisions are under-specified and several choices are defensible. Yet a subtle but scientifically significant error can invalidate the dataset in ways aggregate metrics can miss. We therefore pair outcome-based metrics with a process-based rubric, scored by two human evaluators against manual reference solutions. We find that agents succeed on most subtasks but rarely produce a fully error-free end-to-end solution; we characterize their mistakes and suggest data-sharing practices for agent-assisted reuse. Finally, we find that agent judges are unreliable at catching errors on their own, but can automate process-based evaluation when given reference solutions.
  </details>

- **[Locking Pretrained Weights via Deep Low-Rank Residual Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.10777)**  `arXiv:2605.10777`  
  _Keitaro Sakamoto, Pierre Ablin, Federico Danieli, Marco Cuturi_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  The quality of open-weight language models has dramatically improved in recent years. Sharing weights greatly facilitates model adoption by enabling their use across diverse hardware and software platforms. They also allow for more open research and testing, to the extent that users can use them as checkpoints, fine-tune them according to their needs, and potentially redistribute them. In some cases, however, concerns on modifying these weights towards unauthorized uses may outweigh the pros of giving users such freedom. Defending against such adaptation is non-trivial: since an adaptive attacker can observe all weights and architectures by definition, they can reverse simple structural defenses, and use optimization to defeat the simplest locking mechanisms. In this work, we exploit the inference-training asymmetry of automatic differentiation as a novel defense axis. We propose DLR-Lock, a method where the purveyor of the model purposely replaces each pretrained MLP in their model with a deep low-rank residual network (DLR-Net) of comparable parameter count, forcing activation memory that grows linearly with depth during backpropagation. DLR-Nets are efficiently trained via module-wise regression. We show that, beyond this memory overhead, DLR-Lock results in architectural mismatches that complicate the optimization landscape of standard fine-tuning, and a backward pass that incurs disproportionately more overhead than the forward pass. Our defense succeeds in withstanding adaptive attackers with full knowledge of the defense strategy while preserving the original model's capabilities. Experiments on LLMs validate these claims.
  </details>

- **[TabFORGE: A Tabular Foundation Model for Generative Modelling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09424)**  `arXiv:2605.09424`  
  _Xiangjian Jiang, Mingxuan Liu, Nikola Simidjievski, Tassilo Klein, Mateja Jamnik_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Generative modelling is a demanding test of foundation models, because it requires robust, holistic representation learning for a given data modality, rather than optimisation for a supervised prediction target alone. While recent work on tabular foundation models has achieved remarkable progress in predictive modelling, generative tabular foundation models remain underexplored. Existing tabular foundation generators, in particular, have not yet consistently matched strong dataset-specific generators in synthetic data quality. A key reason is their insufficient alignment with the inter-feature dependency structure of tabular data, which can reflect underlying causal relationships. In this paper, we address this gap by introducing a novel tabular foundation model, $\textbf{TabFORGE}$, built on pretrained $\textbf{Tab}$ular $\textbf{FO}$undational $\textbf{R}$epresentations for $\textbf{GE}$neration. TabFORGE is designed to utilise transferable representations induced by a pretrained structure-aware feature encoder, which captures information useful for characterising inter-feature dependencies. It further decouples latent modelling from decoding through a two-stage design: we first pretrain a score-based diffusion transformer, and then pretrain a denoising-aligned decoder using the denoised latent embeddings. This design elegantly mitigates the distribution shifts in latent embeddings that typically arise between training and inference. We evaluate TabFORGE comprehensively against 22 benchmark methods on 45 real-world datasets. Our results show that TabFORGE effectively learns and leverages generalisable tabular representations, enabling efficient generation of high-quality synthetic tabular data, particularly with strong structural fidelity. Code is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[HAServe: Horizon-Aware Scheduling and Memory Co-Design for Efficient LLM Serving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.08581)**  `arXiv:2605.08581`  
  _Xingyu Qu, Tianhao Lin, Yiqi Li, Zhiyu Chen, Sheng Wang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Online large language model (LLM) services process requests that share context but differ in prefix structure and arrival timing. Finite capacity couples request admission and key-value (KV) retention. This paper addresses one online serving problem: using a unified view of visible demand to choose the feasible joint admission and KV-retention candidate with the lowest predicted latency cost as prefix structures and arrival rates vary. To model this problem, we introduce HorizonSchema, a workload abstraction that connects exact prefix paths, permitted serializations, and released consumers as shared inputs to both decisions. Our analysis shows that useful reuse depends on demand and prefix survival, while service order changes latency even at equal computation. Furthermore, we present HAServe, which turns this abstraction into a scheduling--memory co-design method of systematic optimization for online LLM serving. We implement HAServe on SGLang and evaluate Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 and Llama2-13B on five workloads using eight H100 GPUs. Across the evaluated workloads, HAServe achieves up to $1.14$--$5.90\times$ P99 TTFT speedups and up to $1.08$--$1.44\times$ the throughput, with KV-cache hit rate up to 20.59 percentage points higher than the strongest baseline for each metric and setting.
  </details>

- **[CRAFT: Forgetting-Aware Intervention-Based Adaptation for Continual Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.05732)**  `arXiv:2605.05732`  
  _Md Anwar Hossen, Fatema Siddika, Juan Pablo Munoz, Tanya Roosta, Ali Jannesari_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large language models (LLMs) can learn new tasks through fine-tuning, but learning tasks sequentially often leads to catastrophic forgetting of earlier ones. This paper proposes CRAFT, a continual learning framework that keeps model weights frozen and instead learns low-rank interventions on hidden representations. Similar tasks share an intervention to help knowledge transfer, with similarity judged by how each task alters the model's output distribution rather than by a learned gating network. Within a shared intervention, a Kullback-Leibler (KL) penalty keeps each new task close to the intervention's existing behavior, which limits forgetting of earlier tasks, while a small, task-private intervention in the deepest layers preserves dedicated capacity that later tasks cannot overwrite. The learned interventions also make it possible to identify the task at test time, so task identity labels are not needed. Across multiple benchmarks and model scales, CRAFT improves overall performance and reduces forgetting compared with strong LoRA-based methods, while remaining robust to task ordering.
  </details>

- **[Do LLMs have core beliefs?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.03255)**  `arXiv:2605.03255`  
  _Anna Sokol, Marianna B. Ganapini, Nitesh V. Chawla_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  The rise of Large Language Models (LLMs) has sparked debate about whether these systems exhibit human-level cognition. In this debate, little attention has been paid to a structural component of human cognition: core beliefs, truths that provide a foundation around which we can build a worldview. These commitments usually resist debunking, as abandoning them would represent a fundamental shift in how we see reality. In this paper, we ask whether LLMs hold anything akin to core commitments. Using a probing framework we call Adversarial Dialogue Trees (ADTs) over five domains (science, history, geography, biology, and mathematics), we find that most LLMs fail to maintain a stable worldview. Though some recent models showed improved stability, they still eventually failed to maintain key commitments under conversational pressure. These results document an improvement in argumentative skills across model generations but indicate that all current models lack a key component of human-level cognition.
  </details>

- **[Where to Steer: Input-Dependent Layer Selection for Steering Improves LLM Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.03867)**  `arXiv:2604.03867`  
  _Soham Gadgil, Chris Lin, Su-In Lee_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Steering vectors have emerged as a lightweight and effective approach for aligning large language models (LLMs) at inference time, enabling modulation of model behaviors by shifting intermediate representations toward a target behavior. Many existing steering methods apply interventions at globally fixed locations in an LLM, effectively treating the optimal intervention location as input-invariant. However, representations relevant to a target behavior can be encoded at different LLM layers depending on the input. Theoretically, we show that different inputs may require steering at different layers to achieve alignment with a given behavior. Empirically, we observe that the most effective layer for steering varies substantially between inputs. Motivated by these observations, we introduce \textit{Where to Steer} (W2S), a general framework that adaptively selects intervention layers conditioned on the inputs by learning a mapping from input representations to steering layers. Across multiple LLMs and alignment behaviors, W2S consistently outperforms fixed-layer baselines in both in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings. Our findings suggest that input-dependent layer selection is a key design dimension complementary to methods for steering vector extraction.
  </details>

- **[Learning Not To Interfere: Adapting Experts For Model Merging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.13467)**  `arXiv:2603.13467`  
  _Pratik Ramesh, George Stoica, Arun Iyer, Leshem Choshen, Judy Hoffman_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Model merging has shown that multitask models can be created by directly combining the parameters of different models that are each specialized on tasks of interest. However, models trained independently on distinct tasks often exhibit interference that degrades the merged model's performance. To solve this problem, we formally define the notion of Cross-Task Interference as the drift in the representation of the merged model relative to its constituent models. Reducing cross-task interference is key to improving merging performance. To address this issue, we propose our method, Resolving Interference (RI), a light-weight adaptation framework which disentangles expert models to be functionally orthogonal to the space of other tasks, thereby reducing cross-task interference. RI does this whilst using only unlabeled auxiliary data as input (i.e., no task-data is needed), allowing it to be applied in data-scarce scenarios. RI consistently improves the performance of state-of-the-art merging methods by up to 3.8% and generalization to unseen domains by up to 2.3%. We also find RI to be robust to the source of auxiliary input while being significantly less sensitive to tuning of merging hyperparameters. Our codebase is available at:this https URL
  </details>

- **[3DTCR: Vortex-following generative reconstruction improves tropical cyclone intensity prediction from global AI weather forecasts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.13049)**  `arXiv:2603.13049`  
  _Jun Liu, Xiaohui Zhong, Kai Zheng, Jiarui Li, Yifei Li, Tao Zhou, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Global numerical weather prediction (NWP) and artificial intelligence (AI) models often underestimate tropical cyclone (TC) intensity, partly because coarse grids underresolve fine-scale three-dimensional inner-core structures that influence TC intensity evolution. Kilometer-scale NWP simulations can better resolve these structures but are too costly for operational use, which also makes high-resolution TC data limited. Here we construct a 3-km, TC-centered dataset for 2018--2024 using the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model and develop 3DTCR, a vortex-following generative framework that reconstructs three-dimensional TC structure from FuXi global forecasts. 3DTCR combines conditional flow matching (CFM) with two-stage training to learn a coarse-to-fine mapping from center-aligned reanalysis simulation pairs and then adapt it to forecast inputs through latent space alignment. Evaluated on 2024 western North Pacific (WNP) forecasts, 3DTCR reduces the root mean square error (RMSE) and the magnitude of the mean bias error (MBE) in maximum 10-m wind speed by 36.5% and 60.7% relative to FuXi, and by 8.9% and 28.2% relative to the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts high-resolution system (ECMWF-HRES), respectively. Case studies suggest that reconstructions capture wind gradients between the eye and eyewall, vertical structure of horizontal winds, and vortex asymmetries, while inheriting the FuXi-predicted TC tracks. 3DTCR generates 5-day TC-centered atmospheric fields in approximately 3 minutes on one GPU, whereas a full-basin 3-km WRF simulation takes about 400 hours on 32 CPU cores. These results demonstrate that such a vortex-following generative reconstruction can add localized three-dimensional detail to global forecasts and improve TC intensity prediction without basin-wide kilometer-scale numerical integration.
  </details>

- **[Fractional Rotation, Full Potential? Investigating Performance and Convergence of Partial RoPE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.11611)**  `arXiv:2603.11611`  
  _Mohammad Aflah Khan, Krishna P. Gummadi, Manish Gupta, Abhilasha Ravichander_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Rotary Positional Embedding (RoPE) is widely used in transformers to encode relative positional information, yet the effect of applying RoPE to only a subset of hidden dimensions remains underexplored. This design choice can substantially reduce memory usage, especially at long context lengths. We show that partial RoPE achieves up to 10$\times$ memory savings over standard RoPE cache while maintaining comparable final loss. We systematically study its impact on training dynamics and convergence across architectures, model sizes, sequence lengths, and datasets. Our results reveal that: (1) applying RoPE to only a small fraction of dimensions (around 10\%) matches the convergence of full RoPE; (2) these trends remain consistent across settings; and (3) NoPE (No Positional Encoding) can produce loss spikes, which are mitigated by minimal RoPE usage or QK-Norm application. Overall, our findings highlight partial RoPE as an effective trade-off between efficiency and stability.
  </details>

- **[Size-Transferability of Graph Transformers with Convolutional Positional Encodings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.15239)**  `arXiv:2602.15239`  
  _Javier Porras-Valenzuela, Zhiyang Wang, Teresa Shang, Yusu Wang, Alejandro Ribeiro_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Transformers have achieved remarkable success across domains, motivating the rise of Graph Transformers (GTs) as attention-based architectures for graph-structured data. A key design choice in GTs is the use of Graph Neural Network (GNN)-based positional encodings to incorporate structural information. In this work, we study GTs through the lens of manifold limit models for graph sequences and establish a theoretical connection between GTs with GNN positional encodings and Manifold Neural Networks (MNNs). Building on transferability results for GNNs under manifold convergence, we show that GTs inherit transferability guarantees from their positional encodings. In particular, GTs trained on small graphs provably generalize to larger graphs under mild assumptions. We complement our theory with extensive experiments on standard graph benchmarks, demonstrating that GTs exhibit scalable behavior on par with GNNs. To further show the efficiency in a real-world scenario, we implement GTs for shortest path distance estimation over terrains to better illustrate the efficiency of the transferable GTs. Our results provide new insights into the understanding of GTs and suggest practical directions for efficient training of GTs in large-scale settings.
  </details>

- **[Mitigating Memorization Where It Happens](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.08901)**  `arXiv:2602.08901`  
  _Xuanqi Zhang, Haoyang Shang, Xiaoxiao Li_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large language models (LLMs) can memorize and reproduce training sequences verbatim, raising privacy and copyright concerns. Existing mitigation methods apply interventions uniformly, often degrading performance on the majority of tokens that generalize normally. We study a token-level log-likelihood ratio between a target model and a domain-competent reference with lower exposure to the evaluated sequences. Exposure-controlled experiments support its use for localizing positions associated with sequence-level verbatim recall. Across evaluated settings, a minority of positions carries a disproportionate share of the positive signal, motivating selective activation correction. From the ideal memorization reduction objective, we derive a probe--steer framework which decomposes intervention into a probe that detects memorization-relevant activations and a steer that applies targeted correction only when the probe exceeds a threshold. We propose Gated Subspace Steering (GSS) as its practical instantiation: the optimal probe--steer pair admits a closed-form solution as the leading singular vectors of a gradient-weighted activation matrix. Across four benchmarks, GSS matches or exceeds state-of-the-art memorization reduction while requiring 10--100$\times$ less compute than optimization-based alternatives.
  </details>

- **[TASTE: Task-Aware Out-of-Distribution Detection via Stein Operators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.07640)**  `arXiv:2602.07640`  
  _Michał Kozyra, Gesine Reinert_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Out-of-distribution detection methods are often either data-centric, detecting deviations from the training input distribution irrespective of their effect on a trained model, or model-centric, relying on classifier outputs without explicit reference to data geometry. We propose TASTE (Task-Aware STEin operators): a task-aware framework based on so-called Stein operators, which links distribution shift to the input sensitivity of the model. The resulting operators admit a geometric interpretation as a projection of distribution shift onto the sensitivity field of the model, with theoretical guarantees. Beyond detecting a shift, the construction enables its localisation through a coordinate-wise decomposition, and - for image data - provides interpretable per-pixel diagnostics. Experiments on controlled Gaussian shifts, MNIST under geometric perturbations, and CIFAR-10/ImageNet-1K perturbed benchmarks demonstrate that TASTE aligns closely with task degradation while showing competitive performance compared to established baselines, with gains that depend on the shift regime.
  </details>

- **[The impact of temporal resampling on the safety of clinical reinforcement learning: A simulated trial](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.06603)**  `arXiv:2602.06603`  
  _Thomas Frost, Hrisheekesh Vaidya, Steve Harris_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Reinforcement learning (RL) is a type of artificial intelligence for making optimal choices. In healthcare, researchers generally use offline RL (ORL), where models are trained and evaluated from retrospective observational data. To accommodate naturally irregular clinical records, researchers often resample the data into uniform time intervals before training (known as binning). However, binning may create counterfactual trajectories that do not represent clinical practice. We first quantified these distortions in patients receiving continuous insulin infusions in the MIMIC-IV intensive care database. Binning reversed the apparent causal order for over 70% of paired glucose measurements and insulin adjustments within the same interval, and frequently masked significant dysglycaemic events and merged distinct treatment decisions together. We then conducted an in silico clinical trial using 30 virtual patients with type 1 diabetes from the FDA-approved UVA/Padova simulator. The simulator was modified to include stochastic intervals between decisions and used to generate a training dataset for offline RL. We trained three ORL algorithms on both the unprocessed dataset and equivalent datasets resampled at 10-minute, 2-hour, and 4-hour intervals. When deployed back into the simulated environment, temporal resampling was found to reduce model performance by up to 60% relative to unprocessed data, with 4-hour binning causing all agents to perform worse than the dataset's baseline. Retrospective evaluation on resampled data actively obscured this effect, predicting 1.5-3x better returns than agents achieved in practice. We recommend that future research in this area prioritises datasets with natural clinical timings between decisions, which may be a necessary step before these models can be safely deployed into patient care.
  </details>

- **[Soft Sensor for Bottom-Hole Pressure Estimation in Petroleum Wells Using Long Short-Term Memory and Transfer Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.03737)**  `arXiv:2602.03737`  
  _M. A. Fernandes, E. Gildin, M. A. Sampaio_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Monitoring bottom-hole variables in petroleum wells is essential for production optimization, safety, and emissions reduction. Permanent Downhole Gauges (PDGs) provide real-time pressure data but face reliability and cost issues. We propose a machine learning-based soft sensor to estimate flowing Bottom-Hole Pressure (BHP) using wellhead and topside measurements. A Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) model is introduced and compared with Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) and Ridge Regression. We also pioneer Transfer Learning for adapting models across operational environments. Tested on real offshore datasets from Brazil's Pre-salt basin, the methodology achieved Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) consistently below 2\%, outperforming benchmarks. This work offers a cost-effective, accurate alternative to physical sensors, with broad applicability across diverse reservoir and flow conditions.
  </details>

- **[Product Interaction: An Algebraic Formalism for Deep Learning Architectures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.02573)**  `arXiv:2602.02573`  
  _Haonan Dong, Chun-Wun Cheng, Angelica I. Aviles-Rivero_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Modern neural architectures are largely developed as distinct empirical constructions, despite recurring principles across convolutional, attention, state-space, and equivariant models. We introduce Product Interactions, an algebraic formalism that unifies these architectures under a common construction principle and turns their design into a systematic procedure. The core shift is representing data as algebraic elements and treating multiplication, rather than linear transformation alone, as a primitive architectural operation. Architectures are generated by composing multiplication operators, with input dependence organized by self-interaction order. Within this formalism, we derive convolutional and equivariant networks as symmetry-constrained first-order product interactions, recover Mamba from state-space models as an increase in self-interaction order from one to three, and establish attention as a third-order interaction from composing the same operator. Equivariance is incorporated by constraining the algebraic product via symmetry: translation equivariance yields convolution, while SO(3)-compatibility produces the Clebsch--Gordan product and tensor-field interactions. This perspective recasts architecture design as an algebraic construction problem: the choice of algebra defines admissible interactions, symmetry constrains their structure, and composition generates higher-order architectures. The framework is thus generative. Following these principles, we construct a simplified-algebra dynamical layer that improves both accuracy and throughput over Mamba on CIFAR-10. Experiments show that interaction order affects accuracy non-monotonically and symmetry constraints boost learnability. Product Interactions provides a mathematical methodology for analyzing existing architectures and systematically designing new ones.
  </details>

- **[TabClustPFN: A Prior-data Fitted Network for Tabular Data Clustering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.21656)**  `arXiv:2601.21656`  
  _Tianqi Zhao, Guanyang Wang, Yan Shuo Tan, Qiong Zhang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Prior-data Fitted Networks (PFNs) have reframed supervised tabular learning as single-pass in-context inference without per-dataset optimization. Extending this paradigm to clustering is appealing yet fundamentally more challenging, due to absent supervision, unknown cluster cardinality, and label switching inherent to partition outputs. Existing PFN-based clustering methods address these challenges only partially, either requiring known cardinality as input or relying on unstable label-ordering conventions and overly restrictive synthetic priors. We introduce TabClustPFN, a clustering PFN that resolves all challenges jointly through co-designed prior, objective, and architecture. Our hybrid pretraining prior captures heterogeneous real-tabular geometry; our decoupled partition inference network--cardinality inference network architecture jointly infers cluster assignments and cardinality in a single pass; and our SoftARI training objective is permutation-invariant by construction, eliminating the need for any label-ordering convention. On a 44 curated real-world tabular benchmark, TabClustPFN achieves state-of-the-art clustering performance against classical, deep, and amortized baselines, with runtime comparable to efficient baselines. Code is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[DeFlow: Decoupling Behavior-Prior Modeling and Value Maximization for Offline Policy Extraction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.10471)**  `arXiv:2601.10471`  
  _Zhancun Mu, Chi Zhang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We present DeFlow, a decoupled offline RL framework that leverages flow matching to faithfully capture complex behavior manifolds. Optimizing generative policies is computationally prohibitive, typically necessitating backpropagation through ODE solvers. We address this by learning a lightweight refinement module within an explicit, data-derived trust region of the flow manifold, rather than sacrificing the iterative generation capability via single-step distillation. This way, we bypass solver differentiation and eliminate the need for balancing loss terms, ensuring stable improvement while fully preserving the flow's iterative expressivity. Empirically, DeFlow achieves superior performance on the challenging OGBench benchmark and demonstrates efficient offline-to-online adaptation.
  </details>

- **[Scientific feedback reveals productive regimes beyond training conventions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.15756)**  `arXiv:2512.15756`  
  _Yoon Pyo Lee, Samrendra Roy, Souvik Chakraborty, Syed Bahauddin Alam_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Human-imposed design conventions can restrict the alternatives represented in scientific training data and shape the search preferences learned by generative models. We show that scientific performance feedback can redirect the learned search distribution toward productive regions beyond those conventions, without explicitly rewarding departures from them. We test this process in reactor lattice design with simulated feedback and chemical reaction-condition selection with measured yields, using a pretrained sequence policy and a small non-language policy, respectively. In both settings, adaptation improves scientific performance while increasing generation of choices excluded from the corresponding supervised data. In measured reactions, probability on task-specific ligand choices excluded from training rises from 0.29 to 0.70-0.71 as expected yield error decreases. Controls in the lattice setting show that the productive region identified during adaptation provides reusable information to random search, while aligned generation produces useful candidates more frequently than informed random sampling. Removing the target penalty redirects four of five matched runs, linking the direction of adaptation to the scientific objective. Together, these results show how scientific feedback reshapes inherited search preferences and reveals productive alternatives beyond training conventions, with attribution controls distinguishing learned redistribution from candidate availability and reusable search information.
  </details>

- **[CarBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Neural Surrogates on High-Fidelity 3D Car Aerodynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.07847)**  `arXiv:2512.07847`  
  _Mohamed Elrefaie, Dule Shu, Matt Klenk, Faez Ahmed_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Benchmarking has been the cornerstone of progress in computer vision, natural language processing, and the broader deep learning domain, driving algorithmic innovation through standardized datasets and reproducible evaluation protocols. The growing availability of large-scale Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) datasets has opened new opportunities for applying machine learning to aerodynamic and engineering design. Yet, despite this progress, there exists no standardized benchmark for large-scale numerical simulations in engineering design. In this work, we introduce CarBench, the first comprehensive benchmark dedicated to large-scale 3D car aerodynamics, performing a large-scale evaluation of state-of-the-art models on DrivAerNet++, the largest public dataset for automotive aerodynamics, containing over 8,000 high-fidelity car simulations. We assess eleven architectures spanning neural operator methods (e.g., Fourier Neural Operator), geometric deep learning (PointNet, RegDGCNN, PointMAE, PointTransformer), transformer-based neural solvers (Transolver, Transolver++, AB-UPT), and implicit field networks (TripNet). Beyond standard interpolation tasks, we perform cross-category experiments in which transformer-based solvers trained on a single car archetype are evaluated on unseen categories. Our analysis covers predictive accuracy, physical consistency, computational efficiency, and statistical uncertainty. To accelerate progress in data-driven engineering, we open-source the benchmark framework, including training pipelines, uncertainty estimation routines based on bootstrap resampling, and pretrained model weights, establishing the first reproducible foundation for large-scale learning from high-fidelity CFD simulations, available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[AlignSAE: Concept-Aligned Sparse Autoencoders](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.02004)**  `arXiv:2512.02004`  
  _Minglai Yang, Xinyu Guo, Zhengliang Shi, Jinhe Bi, Steven Bethard, Mihai Surdeanu, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large Language Models (LLMs) encode factual knowledge within hidden parametric spaces that are difficult to inspect or control. While Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) can decompose hidden activations into more fine-grained, interpretable features, they often struggle to reliably align these features with human-defined concepts, resulting in entangled and distributed feature representations. To address this, we introduce AlignSAE, a method that aligns SAE features with a predefined ontology through a "pre-train, then post-train" curriculum. After an initial unsupervised training phase, we apply supervised post-training to bind specific concepts to dedicated latent slots while preserving the remaining capacity for general reconstruction. This separation creates an interpretable interface where specific concepts can be inspected and controlled without interference from unrelated features. Empirical results on GPT-2 across synthetic biographical QA (1-hop, 6 concepts) and compositional relational reasoning (2-hop, 20 concepts) demonstrate that AlignSAE enables precise causal interventions, such as reliable concept swaps (94.8% success in 1-hop), by targeting single, semantically aligned slots. AlignSAE achieves disentanglement improvements of $9$--$\infty\times$ over standard SAEs (measured via Mutual Information Gap), and further supports multi-hop reasoning and a mechanistic probe of grokking-like generalization dynamics. Although our evaluation focuses on GPT-2, AlignSAE itself is model-agnostic.
  </details>

- **[Graph Homomorphism Distortion: A structural (pseudo)-metric for attributed graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.03068)**  `arXiv:2511.03068`  
  _Martin Carrasco, Olga Zaghen, Kavir Sumaraj, Erik Bekkers, Bastian Rieck_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  A large driver of the complexity of graph learning is the interplay between structure and features. When analyzing the expressivity of graph neural networks, however, existing approaches ignore features in favor of structure, making it nigh-impossible to assess to what extent two graphs with close features should be considered similar. We address this by developing a new (pseudo-)metric based on graph homomorphisms Inspired by concepts from metric geometry, our graph homomorphism distortion measures the minimal worst-case distortion that node features of one graph are subjected to when mapping one graph to another. We demonstrate the utility of our (pseudo-)metric by showing that i.) it can be efficiently approximated while retaining distinction capabilities, ii.) it provides a granular approach to graph distinction, and, iii.) it serves as a structural encoding, extending the concept of homomorphism-based descriptors to attributed graphs, thus improving the predictive capabilities of graph neural networks.
  </details>

- **[Thinking-Free Policy Initialization Makes Distilled Reasoning Models More Effective and Efficient Reasoners](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.26226)**  `arXiv:2509.26226`  
  _Xin Xu, Clive Bai, Kai Yang, Tianhao Chen, Yang Wang, Saiyong Yang, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Reward (RLVR) effectively solves complex tasks but demands extremely long context lengths during training, leading to substantial computational costs. While multi-stage training can partially mitigate this, starting with overly short contexts often causes irreversible performance degradation, ultimately failing to reduce overall training compute significantly. In this paper, we introduce Thinking-Free Policy Initialization (TFPI), a simple yet effective adaptation to RLVR that bridges long Chain-of-Thought (CoT) distillation and standard RLVR. TFPI employs a simple ThinkingFree operation, explicitly discarding the thinking content via a direct </think> append, to reduce token usage during inference. Training with ThinkingFree-adapted inputs improves performance and lowers token consumption, even in the original slow-thinking mode. Extensive experiments across various benchmarks have shown that TFPI accelerates RL convergence, achieves a higher performance ceiling, and yields more token-efficient reasoning models without specialized rewards or complex training designs. With TFPI only, we train a 4B model to reach 89.0% accuracy on AIME24 and 65.5% on LiveCodeBench using less than 4K H20 hours.
  </details>

- **[Stabilizing the Modality Gap: Null-Space Projected Continual Learning for Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.19839)**  `arXiv:2507.19839`  
  _Tiantian Peng, Yuyang Liu, Shuo Yang, Qiuhe Hong, YongHong Tian_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  The modality gap is intrinsic to multimodal alignment, where embeddings from different modalities remain partially separated in a shared representation space. In continual learning, CLIP-based vision-language models (VLMs) not only suffer catastrophic forgetting but also experience modality gap drift that disrupts the shared embedding geometry. Such drift degrades cross-modal alignment and generalization. We propose FPCD, an efficient framework combining Fast Null-space Projection (FNP) and Contrastive Distillation (CD). FNP accumulates compact Gram matrices of previous tasks' activations and projects gradients onto layer-adaptive approximate null spaces to reduce interference with learned representations. By replacing singular value decomposition with symmetric eigendecomposition, FNP accelerates projection-basis construction by a factor of 5-9. CD uses a small reference set to align the bidirectional image-to-text and text-to-image similarity distributions of the fine-tuned model with CLIP, thereby preserving pretrained cross-modal relations. On the 11-task MTIL benchmark, FPCD achieves 87.6% Last, 76.4% Average, and 65.2% Transfer. It also maintains more stable modality gaps and stronger zero-shot retrieval performance on COCO Captions and Flickr30k than competing methods. These results highlight the importance of controlling modality gap drift during continual adaptation of VLMs.
  </details>

- **[HERO: Preserving Structure and Semantics in Heterogeneous Continual Graph Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.17458)**  `arXiv:2505.17458`  
  _Guiquan Sun, Xikun Zhang, Jingchao Ni, Dongjin Song_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Machine learning on heterogeneous graphs has advanced rapidly, driven by the diverse entities, relations, and semantics inherent in real-world data. However, most existing studies assume static graphs, whereas real-world graph data are often continuously updated. Continual learning in this setting is particularly challenging because historical knowledge is encoded not only in target-node representations, but also in their heterogeneous structural contexts and relation-dependent semantic responses. To this end, we introduce HERO, a heterogeneous continual graph learning framework that preserves historical knowledge at both structural and semantic levels while adapting to incoming tasks. We analyze experience replay as an approximation to the unavailable historical gradient and decompose its error into target-selection and context-reconstruction terms. This analysis shows that replaying target nodes alone is generally insufficient for relation-sensitive HGNNs, as removing typed neighborhood context can alter both representations and historical gradients. Motivated by this, HERO employs DiSCo to select representative target nodes and reconstruct compact heterogeneous contexts through relation-aware multi-type neighbor expansion. To further preserve knowledge that cannot be captured by replayed subgraphs alone, HERO aligns task-conditioned predictions and heterogeneous semantic responses through multi-level knowledge distillation. A lightweight look-ahead adaptation step is additionally used to improve plasticity on incoming tasks. Experiments on four datasets with three HGNN backbones show that HERO achieves the best or tied-best average performance among state-of-the-art baselines, while maintaining competitive forgetting. Our code is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[KnowEEG: Explainable Knowledge Driven EEG Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.00541)**  `arXiv:2505.00541`  
  _Amarpal Sahota, Navid Mohammadi Foumani, Raul Santos-Rodriguez, Zahraa S. Abdallah_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Electroencephalography (EEG) classification has shown significant promise in applications ranging from neurodegenerative disease detection to brain-computer interfaces (BCIs). Whilst deep learning methods have increasingly dominated the research landscape in recent years; these models remain largely opaque 'black boxes' with limited interpretability. In this paper, we revisit the utility of feature-based classification via a systematic pipeline designed to integrate per-electrode signal statistics with cross-brain connectivity metrics. The proposed "KnowEEG" pipeline extracts 783 per-electrode statistical features alongside between-electrode connectivity statistics, utilizing a balanced sampling strategy between high-dimensional per electrode features and connectivity. This feature-based pipeline achieves performance comparable to or exceeding state-of-the-art deep learning models across five diverse classification tasks: emotion detection, mental workload classification, eyes open/closed detection, abnormal EEG classification, and event detection. This performance is achieved without the need for Graphics Processing Unit (GPU) resources. Furthermore, the pipeline provides inherent explainability through feature importance rankings. We demonstrate via the eyes open/closed task that this explainability identifies discriminative biomarkers in the occipital region that are consistent with established neuroscience literature. These results suggest that despite significant advances in deep learning, structured feature engineering remains a high performance and interpretable method for EEG classification.
  </details>

- **[FANTF: Fuzzy attention network based transformers for time series analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.00070)**  `arXiv:2504.00070`  
  _Sanjay Chakraborty, Fredrik Heintz_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  This paper introduces Fuzzy Attention Network-Based Transformer (FANTF), an approach for time series forecasting, classification, and anomaly detection. FANTF combines fuzzy logic concepts with transformer architectures through a novel fuzzy attention mechanism. The proposed mechanism is inspired by Type-2 fuzzy set theory. It uses a learnable Gaussian uncertainty perturbation to model uncertainty in attention relevance scores. This makes it possible for the model to accurately capture uncertainty in temporal relationships better than normal deterministic attention. Transformers capacity to record complex temporal patterns and multivariate connections is enhanced by FANTF. The approach is both architecture-agnostic and task-agnostic. The proposed fuzzy attention module can be used as a direct replacement for the standard attention layer. To evaluate its effectiveness, FANTF is integrated into five transformer backbones: Transformer, Informer, PatchTST, Crossformer, and iTransformer. The fuzzy attention mechanism produces softer and more diverse attention distributions. It provides uncertainty-aware interpretations through attention heatmap visualizations. Experimental evaluations on some real-life datasets reveal that FANTF enhances the forecasting performance, classification, and anomaly detection tasks over traditional transformer-based models. FANTF achieves statistically significant and competitive performance improvements over standard transformer-based baselines on most benchmark datasets (p < 0.05, Wilcoxon signed-rank test), observed under noisy and non-stationary time series conditions.
  </details>

- **[Pairwise Difference Learning for Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.20031)**  `arXiv:2406.20031`  
  _Mohamed Karim Belaid, Maximilian Rabus, Eyke Hüllermeier_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Pairwise difference learning (PDL) has recently been introduced as a new meta-learning technique for regression. Instead of learning a mapping from instances to outcomes in the standard way, the key idea is to learn a function that takes two instances as input and predicts the difference between the respective outcomes. Given a function of this kind, predictions for a query instance are derived from every training example and then averaged. This paper extends PDL toward the task of classification and proposes a meta-learning technique for inducing a PDL classifier by solving a suitably defined (binary) classification problem on a paired version of the original training data. We analyze the performance of the PDL classifier in a large-scale empirical study and find that it outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of prediction performance. Last but not least, we provide an easy-to-use and publicly available implementation of PDL in a Python package.
  </details>

- **[Learning Self-Orchestration in Decentralized Agent Swarms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22322)**  `arXiv:2610.22322`

  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  The capabilities of an agent swarm depend on both its individual members and how they coordinate. Learning both action and bidding behavior allows individual capabilities and patterns of participation to adapt together without a central coordinating agent. We evaluate MPT on embodied crafting, robot navigation, and deep research. Results show gains over monolithic post-training and confirm that agent participation indeed evolves with learning. With the same post-trained action policies, learned self-orchestration outperforms alternative coordination strategies. Ablations show that both action and bidding benefit from learning, and that learned bids provide more effective action-training signals. Beyond the original training objectives, trained swarms adapt faster to related tasks and achieve better performance with larger populations at inference time. Larger populations also suffer smaller performance losses under agent dropout, demonstrating that learned self-orchestration supports reuse, scaling, and robustness in decentralized agent swarms. - **[Agentic-Priors: Using Large Language Models to Address the Cold Start Problem in Preference Elicitation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21938)**  `arXiv:2610.21938`  
  _Bruno Arcanjo, Zhaoxing Li, Sebastian Stein_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  An agent that learns a user's preferences from their choices faces a cold start problem: before any choices are observed, it must rely solely on a prior. Informative priors are usually fitted to historical choice data, which new tasks and deployments lack. To address this, we present Agentic-Priors, which lets agentic systems use the implicit knowledge of large language models (LLMs) instead. Specifically, an LLM states a new user's trade-offs in interpretable terms, such as willingness to pay or value of time, which we map to a prior over multinomial logit coefficients. This prior is then refined by a Bayesian learner as choices are observed. Across seven choice datasets, Agentic-Priors improves cold start accuracy over an uninformed prior by 5-40 percentage points. It also outperforms AutoElicit, a state-of-the-art LLM prior-elicitation method, on three datasets and loses on one. It is up to 18 points more accurate than in-context learning, and never significantly worse.
